summary.text: A bacteriophage, or phage, is a virus that infects and replicates within bacteria, and its name joins a Greek word meaning to devour with the word bacteria.
Phages are proteins wrapped around a DNA or RNA genome, and they are found wherever bacteria exist, among the most common and diverse entities in the biosphere.
Phages have been used as an alternative to antibiotics, and they are seen as a possible therapy against multi-drug-resistant strains of many bacteria.

paragraphs.heading: Viruses that eat bacteria
paragraphs.text: A bacteriophage, or phage for short, is a virus that infects bacteria and multiplies inside them. Its name joins the Greek word for 'to devour' with the word bacteria. A phage is made of proteins wrapped around a genome of DNA or RNA, and that genome may hold as few as four genes or as many as hundreds. To reproduce, a phage injects its genome into a bacterium's cytoplasm and replicates there.

paragraphs.heading: Everywhere bacteria are
paragraphs.text: Phages turn up wherever bacteria exist, and they are among the most common and varied entities in the biosphere. There may be more than 10³¹ of them on the planet, outnumbering all the planet's living organisms, bacteria included, put together. In the water of the world's oceans, no biological entity is more plentiful than viruses, with up to 9×10⁸ virions per millilitre found in microbial mats at the surface. Phages may infect as many as 70% of the bacteria in the sea.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery
paragraphs.text: On 3 September 1917, Félix d'Hérelle, a French-Canadian microbiologist at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, announced an invisible microbe that worked against the dysentery bacillus. He concluded that the clear spots he had seen were caused by a virus living as a parasite on bacteria, and he named it a bacteriophage, a bacterium-eater. He also described a man with dysentery who was restored to health by phages. D'Hérelle went on to introduce the idea of phage therapy, and in 1919 in Paris he made the first clinical use of a phage.

paragraphs.heading: Rise and fall of phage therapy
paragraphs.text: From the 1920s, the Soviet Union and Central Europe, as well as France and Brazil, used phages as an alternative to antibiotics. In Soviet Georgia, Giorgi Eliava pioneered their use against bacterial infections in the 1920s and 1930s, with help from d'Hérelle. Antibiotics, once discovered and widely marketed, were easier to make, store and prescribe. Soviet research appeared mostly in Russian or Georgian and for years was not followed abroad, and the red scare led to the Soviet approach being discouraged and sometimes banned.

paragraphs.heading: A second look
paragraphs.text: Phages are now seen as a possible therapy against bacteria that resist many drugs. Since the Cold War ended, Russia, Georgia and other parts of Central and Eastern Europe have kept using them. In June 2009 the first regulated, randomised, double-blind clinical trial was reported, testing a phage cocktail on infected leg ulcers, and the FDA approved it as a Phase I trial. The results showed the treatment was safe but did not show that it worked. The authors suggested that chemicals from standard wound care, such as lactoferrin or silver, may have interfered with the phages' viability.

paragraphs.heading: Nobel-winning science
paragraphs.text: In 1969, Max Delbrück, Alfred Hershey and Salvador Luria won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries about how viruses replicate and about their genetic structure. Hershey's part in the 1952 Hershey–Chase experiment gave convincing evidence that DNA, not protein, is the genetic material of life. Delbrück and Luria showed statistically that mutations in bacteria happen at random, fitting Darwin's ideas rather than Lamarck's. In 2018, George Smith and Gregory Winter won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for phage display of peptides and antibodies.
